t.3.23.1: As Khara of fierce prowess advanced toward the hermitage, Rāma, together with his brother, beheld those very same ominous portents.
t.3.23.2: Seeing those portents arisen, most dreadful, hair-raising, and harmful to all creatures, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.23.3: O mighty-armed one, behold these great portents that have arisen, destroyers of all beings, to bring about the annihilation of all the rākṣasas.
t.3.23.4: Those harsh clouds, ruddy-grey like donkeys, roll across the sky, pouring down streams of blood and sending forth grating roars.
t.3.23.5: All my arrows, eager for battle, are giving off smoke, and the gold-backed bows are quivering, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.23.6: Judging by the way the forest-roaming birds are crying here, danger has come upon us ahead, and there is peril to our very lives.
t.3.23.7: A very great battle will surely take place, there is no doubt; this arm of mine, throbbing again and again, tells me so.
t.3.23.8: O hero, in the coming clash it portends victory for us and defeat for the enemy, for your face is seen to be radiant and serene.
t.3.23.10: A wise man who desires his own welfare and foresees danger should make provision in advance for what has not yet come.
t.3.23.9: For those who, having risen up for battle, find Lakṣmaṇa standing against them, their faces become lustreless and their lives come to an end.
t.3.23.11: Therefore, taking Vaidehī with you, arrows in hand and bow held ready, take refuge in a cave of the mountain, one hard to reach and thick with trees.
t.3.23.12: I do not wish this word of mine to be opposed by you; you are adjured by my feet. Go, dear child, without delay.
t.3.23.13: Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, taking up his arrows and bow, withdrew with Sītā to a cave that was hard to reach.
t.3.23.14: When Lakṣmaṇa had entered the cave together with Sītā, Rāma said, "Ah, now all is well arranged," and put on his armor.
t.3.23.15: Adorned with that fire-like armour, Rāma appeared like a smokeless fire risen up in the darkness.
t.3.23.16: Raising his mighty bow and taking up his arrows, that valiant one stood firm there, filling the directions with the twanging of his bowstring.
t.3.23.17: Then the gods together with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas along with the Cāraṇas, and the Guhyakas, greatly terrified, spoke to one another.
t.3.23.18: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds, and Rāma, whose soul is righteous, alone: how will this battle turn out?
t.3.23.19: Then the army of the Yātudhānas, deep-roaring and bristling with dreadful armor, weapons and banners, was seen on every side.
t.3.23.20: Of those who were letting loose lion-like roars, bellowing at one another, stretching their bows to twang them, and yawning again and again.
t.3.23.21: The tremendous uproar of those who raised loud cries and beat their kettledrums filled that forest.
t.3.23.22: Terrified by that sound, the beasts of prey roaming the forest fled to where it was silent, and they did not look behind them.
t.3.23.23: But that army of great speed, bearing many kinds of weapons, deep and like the ocean, advanced toward Rāma.
t.3.23.24: Rāma too, skilled in battle, casting his eyes in every direction, beheld that army of Khara, poised and advancing toward the fight.
t.3.23.25: Stretching his fearsome bow and drawing arrows from his quiver, he summoned up a fierce wrath for the slaying of all the Rākṣasas.
t.3.23.26: Enraged, he became hard to look upon, blazing like the fire at the end of an age. Seeing him filled with fiery energy, the deities of the forest trembled in distress.
t.3.23.27: Then the form of that enraged Rāma appeared like that of Pinākin when he rose up to destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
